newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban orders correspondents to ramshackle hotel.
newsitem.headline: Taleban orders correspondents to ramshackle hotel.

text.p: Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban militia has revived a communist law to force visiting journalists to move into Kabul's ramshackle Continental Hotel.
The aim, a junior tourism minister said, was to gain control of the journalists' "security" and secondly to earn revenue for the dilapidated hotel, which has seen better days.
A statement read out on Taleban-controlled radio in Kabul on Friday night said journalists were obliged to move to the hotel.
"The hotel management requests that foreign guests, such as journalists and other foreign nationals staying in...rented accommodation, should contact the Continental Hotel," the statement said.
"They are not allowed to stay anywhere else."

Officials of the ministry of civil aviation and tourism said the statement had been prepared by the management of the Continental Hotel and cleared for broadcast by the deputy head of the Taleban's interim ruling council in Kabul, Mullah Mohammed Hassan.
The deputy minister of civil aviation and tourism said there were two reasons behind reviving the law.
"The first aim of Taleban policy regarding journalists' accommodation is to establish Taleban control over journalist's security arrangements," said deputy minister Mullah Hamdullah.
"The second objective is to strengthen the economy of the hotel," he told Reuters on Saturday morning.

The law stating that journalists could only stay in approved accommodation was first put on the statute books by the communist regime. It was designed exert a degree of control over journalist's activities.
Although the same law existed under the previous administration, it was rarely enforced.
The Taleban have also revived a law requiring exit visas for all visitors on single entry visas.
The Continental -- formerly Intercontinental -- was once the queen of Kabul's hostelries, but is now a sorry shadow of its former self.
Only 85 of the hotel's 200 rooms are habitable.
One side of the hotel has been extensively damages by rocket and shell fire. Over many of the windows are thin sheets of polythene where there had once been glass.
Heavily armed Taleban militiamen sit in the cavernous lobby, one end of which has been shattered by a rocket strike.
The reception desk has leaflets advertising Westminster Abbey in London and the joys of Intourist, the Soviet Union's travel agency.

The hotel charges $60 a night for a single room and boasts 14 hours a day of electricity, lifts that do not work and a restaurant with a wide-ranging menu, of which only one item is normally available.

The Taleban hope to re-build the hotel's former glory, but say it must be run according to the lines of the puritanical vision of Islam that they have imposed on the 75 per cent of the country they control.

They have banned music, dancing, alcohol and mixed swimming, something that might discourage the hundreds of high-spending tourists that thronged the hotel's discos, bars and swimming pool before the war.
Responding to an enquiry on Saturday afternoon, the hotel's receptionist said they would have no trouble accommodating any journalists who wished to stay.
He said that if we cared to book for a whole year, we would be entitled to a discount.
